Main Contributions | # | Contribution | |---|--------------| | **C1** | Introduces an **iterative “Self‑Refine” pipeline** for automated exam authoring. A large language model (OpenAI o3‑mini) alternates between generating a MC‑question, judging it as *good* or *bad*, and feeding the labelled example back into the prompt. This loop continues until 20 acceptable items are collected. | | **C2** | Shows how to **tailor questions to any college course** by feeding instructor‑provided materials (syllabus, description, past homework/exams) into both the generator and the judge. | | **C3** | Conducts one of the **largest real‑world evaluations of AI‑generated items** to date: 71 courses (≈1 200 students) received AI‑written exams; 20 statistics courses (≈ 500 students) received exams assembled from an AP‑Statistics question bank (human‑written) as a benchmark. | | **C4** | Provides a **psychometric (IRT) analysis** of the items, comparing difficulty, discrimination, and overall test information between AI‑generated and human‑written questions. | | **C5** | Openly releases the prompt templates, pseudo‑code, and a full example exam, enabling replication and extension. | --- ### 2. Methodology | Step | Process | |------|---------| | **2.1 Materials collection** | Instructors submit plain‑text versions of course description, syllabus, and any prior assessments. | | **2.2 Prompt design** | Two prompt families: (a) *generator* – asks the model to produce a single MC‑question in JSON; (b) *judge* – asks the model to label the question “Keep” (good) or “Remove” (bad) based on appropriateness, relevance, and non‑triviality. Few‑shot examples from a 2012 AP‑Statistics exam are provided as “good” seeds. | | **2.3 Iterative generation** | Loop until 20 “good” items are obtained:
1. Generate a question.
2. Judge it.
3. Append the (question, label) pair to the prompt as a new example (up to 5 good + 5 bad). | | **2.4 Exam assembly** | The 20 good items are re‑judged for difficulty and answer correctness. The 10 hardest (according to the judge) are kept as the final exam. If <10 survive, another batch of 20 is generated and the process repeats. | | **2.5 Benchmark creation** | For the 20 statistics courses, 10 items are selected from a publicly‑available 2012 AP‑Statistics practice test. Selection is driven by an LLM that matches question concepts to each course and orders by increasing difficulty. | | **2.6 Field study** | 182 sections (164 distinct courses) were recruited across U.S. colleges. 121 sections completed the semester‑end exam; after removing pilot‑created exams, 91 sections remained (71 AI, 20 benchmark). All students also took a common pre‑test of quantitative reasoning. | | **2.7 Psychometric analysis** | A Bayesian hierarchical **2‑parameter logistic IRT model** (item discrimination α, difficulty β, latent ability θ) was fit jointly to pre‑test and semester‑end responses, providing a common ability scale. Posterior inference used cmdstanr (4 chains, 1 000 draws each). Convergence diagnostics (Ȓ < 1.05, ESS > 700) and posterior predictive checks confirmed model fit. | --- ### 3. Key Findings | Metric | AI‑Generated Items | Human/Standard Items | Observation | |--------|--------------------|----------------------|-------------| | **Difficulty (β)** | Mean ≈ ‑0.45 (easier). ~60 % of responses correct. | Mean ≈ +0.35 (harder). ~39 % correct. | AI items were deliberately easier, likely because the generation loop favored concepts that matched the course materials. | | **Discrimination (α)** | Mean ≈ 1.30 (moderate‑high). 31 % “high/very‑high”. | Mean ≈ 1.20 (moderate). 21 % “high/very‑high”. | AI items were slightly more discriminating; posterior difference δα = 0.09 (95 % CI ‑0.09–0.25), with Pr(α_AI > α_STD) ≈ 0.85. | | **Test information** | Max I ≈ 3.85 → reliability R ≈ 0.79; peak at θ ≈ ‑0.51 (best for below‑average ability). | Max I ≈ 2.61 → reliability R ≈ 0.72; peak at θ ≈ +0.32 (best for above‑average ability). | | **Overall reliability** | Across the ability range (θ < 0.75) AI exams provided **greater information** than benchmark exams. | | **Practical outcome** | 10‑question AI exams can be produced in < 5 min of model calls per course and achieve psychometric quality comparable to well‑curated standardized items. | --- ### 4. Limitations & Future Directions * Benchmark limited to courses because suitable public item banks for other domains are scarce. * Only multiple‑choice format was examined; the pipeline could be extended to short‑answer or open‑response items with LLM grading. * Exams were deliberately short (10 items) to limit participant burden; scaling to longer assessments remains to be tested. * The “human” reference condition involved LLM‑mediated selection of AP items, not fully bespoke expert‑crafted exams. * The IRT analysis assumes a static ability (θ) between pre‑test and semester‑end; differential learning gains across conditions could bias comparisons. Future work suggested: (1) randomised assignment of AI vs. expert exams across many subjects; (2) fine‑tuning LLMs on student‑response data to directly target desired difficulty/discrimination; (3) integration with adaptive testing platforms; (4) multilingual and culturally‑adapted question generation. --- ### 5. Take‑away The study demonstrates that **an iterative LLM‑refinement loop can autonomously generate high‑quality, course‑specific multiple‑choice questions** whose **psychometric properties rival or exceed those of human‑written standardized items**, while requiring dramatically less expert time. This positions generative AI as a viable tool for scaling personalized assessment in higher education. Candidate B: ### Summary of the Research Paper **Title:** Iterative Refinement for Generating High-Quality, Customized Exam Questions with Generative AI **Main Contributions:** 1. **Iterative Refinement Strategy:** The study introduces an iterative refinement strategy for generating exam questions tailored to specific course content, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs). 2. **Large-Scale Field Study:** It conducts one of the largest field studies of AI-generated assessments, evaluating 71 college courses with approximately 1,200 students. 3. **Benchmarking:** The performance of AI-generated questions is benchmarked against human-created questions from a standardized Advanced Placement (AP) exam. **Methodology:** - **Data Collection:** Instructor-provided course materials are used to generate context-specific questions. - **Question Generation Process:** A two-stage, iterative process is employed: - **Stage 1:** Generate and evaluate questions until 20 "good" questions are labeled by an AI-judge. - **Stage 2:** Evaluate the appropriateness and difficulty of these 20 questions, selecting the 10 hardest to form the final exam. - **AI Model Used:** OpenAI's o3-mini model is utilized for both question generation and evaluation. - **Evaluation Framework:** Item Response Theory (IRT) is applied to assess the quality of the generated questions in terms of difficulty and discriminatory power. **Key Findings:** 1. **Quality Parity:** AI-generated questions performed on par with expert-created questions, showing similar difficulty and discriminatory power. 2. **Slightly Easier but More Discriminating:** On average, AI-generated questions were slightly easier but more discriminating than those created by human experts. 3. **Test Information and Reliability:** AI-generated exams provided higher test information and reliability, particularly for students with below-average ability. 4. **Potential for Scalability:** The findings suggest that generative AI can produce high-quality, customized assessments at scale, potentially reducing instructor workloads and increasing access to personalized education. **Discussion:** - **Limitations:** The study is limited to multiple-choice questions and short exams, and the comparison is primarily within statistics-related courses. - **Future Work:** Expanding the approach to other subjects, question types, and longer assessments could further validate the potential of AI-assisted question generation. - **Broader Implications:** AI-assisted question generation could enhance educational access, improve learning outcomes through tailored instruction, and facilitate adaptive practice. **Conclusion:** The research demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of using generative AI to create high-quality, customized exam questions, highlighting its potential to transform educational assessment practices.
